By ELIZABETH TROUTMAN MITCHELL, The Daily Signal | November 18, 2026
The White House has withdrawn its nomination for Dr. Heidi Overton to serve as commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration.
This means the Republican Senate will likely not have time to confirm a different appointee before Democrats take the majority in January. Overton previously served as deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council.
“Make America Healthy Again” advocates are chalking the withdrawal up to a win for the movement.
“The truth is MAHA won,” influencer Alex Clark Voetberg said on X.
MAHA influencer Vani Hari, also known as the “Food Babe,” also celebrated the personnel change.
Calley Means, former senior adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., recently told podcast host Joe Rogan that Overton stood in the way of the MAHA agenda. He noted her work on a case that went before the Supreme Court involving liability protections for pesticide manufacturers.
Overton “worked with the Department of Justice to construct a legal argument about why the Supreme Court could take the case and why they should be supporting liability protection for the pesticide makers, and she did not consult [Health and Human Services Secretary] Bobby Kennedy on that,” Means claimed.
“Heidi Overton was the biggest block to MAHA policies I encountered in the government,” he told CBS News’ “Face the Nation” Nov. 8. “On healthy food, on mental health treatments like psychedelics, she was a stone wall.”
Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., outgoing chair of the Senate health committee, wrote on X Tuesday night that the White House “abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton.”
“The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass,” he wrote. “This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate. My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk.”
Pro-life senators wanted assurance that the administration was committed to life issues, which was the last outstanding issue with Overton’s confirmation, Cassidy noted.
Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America had urged the Senate to delay Overton’s confirmation until the FDA committed to cracking down on the abortion pill.
“The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments. Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats,” Cassidy said.
The Senate has not confirmed a new FDA commissioner since Dr. Marty Makary stepped down from the role in May. Kyle Diamantas has served as acting commissioner during that time.
Elizabeth Troutman Mitchell is the White House correspondent for the Daily Signal.

White House Withdraws Nomination of Heidi Overton for FDA Commissioner
The White House on Tuesday pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), after pro-life groups and Senators raised concerns over the Trump administration’s failure to restrict use of the abortion pill.
President Trump nominated Dr. Overton to lead the FDA in August, following the resignation of Commissioner Marty Makary, who left the post in May. Attorney Kyle Diamantas has served as FDA acting commissioner ever since, including while the Senate considered Dr. Overton’s nomination.
“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass,” wrote U.S. Senator Bill Cassidy, who is leaving office in January and chairs the Senate health committee. “This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate.”
When President Trump first selected Dr. Overton to head the FDA, she was seen as a solid pick who is friendly to the pro-life movement.
In 2022, she called the Dobbs decision and the overturning of Roe v. Wade “a huge victory for life.” She added, “Human life is not disposable, but a precious gift from God with inherent worth and dignity.”
At the same time, in a column for The Daily Caller, Dr. Overton criticized the Biden administration’s Department of Health and Human Services detailing the various stages of human development during pregnancy and simultaneously supporting abortion up until birth.
“It should be clear where the radicalism lies,” Dr. Overton wrote. “Americans should reject abortion radicalism and require policies informed by 21st century science and medicine. Then, indeed, we would all be ‘Following the Science!’”
Despite Dr. Overton’s pro-life views, several pro-life organizations and leaders demanded the Senate not confirm her until she committed to restoring safeguards on the abortion pill, like stopping mifepristone from being sent through the mail.
“Dr. Heidi Overton [must] commit to restoring the safeguards governing mifepristone that existed before the Biden administration while the FDA completes its ongoing review of the drug,” 50 leading pro-life groups wrote in a joint statement.
The groups’ frustration stems from the Trump administration’s failure to crack down on the abortion pill, rather than with Dr. Overton herself.
The FDA initially launched a study into mifepristone’s safety in 2025, which was reportedly set to conclude in September 2026. But the study’s release has been delayed to at least March 2027. In the meantime, thousands of women are put at risk and preborn children are killed.
Last year, a study by the Ethics and Public Policy Center (EPPC) found that nearly 11% of all women who abort their children with mifepristone suffer from serious health complications, including sepsis, infection or hemorrhaging.
But to date, the Trump administration’s FDA has not changed mifepristone’s regulations, even after the Biden administration’s FDA allowed mifepristone to be sent through the mail and dispensed at retail pharmacies like Walgreens.
Before her nomination was withdrawn, Dr. Overton had been making progress in persuading Senators to confirm her, Senator Cassidy shared.
“[But] pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues [before confirming her],” Cassidy said. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments. Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”
Only weeks remain before the 120th U.S. Congress begins on January 3, 2027, and Democrats regain control of both the House and Senate.
Since whoever President Trump selects to serve as the next FDA commissioner will have to be confirmed by a Democrat-controlled Senate, it’s very unlikely a nominee friendly to the pro-life movement will take the reins at the FDA.
To truly “follow the science” and “Make America Healthy Again,” the FDA must reinstate safety guardrails on the abortion pill.

Trump Administration Withdraws Heidi Overton’s FDA Nomination Following Bipartisan Senate Opposition
The White House has withdrawn Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration after growing opposition from Republican and Democratic senators threatened her chances of confirmation.
The decision came Tuesday evening, just one day before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee was scheduled to vote on advancing her nomination.
A senior administration official confirmed that Overton lacked sufficient congressional support to move forward, prompting President Trump’s administration to abandon the confirmation effort.
Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated in August to replace former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, who resigned in May.
Her nomination encountered resistance over several issues, including childhood vaccination policies, abortion medication, flavored vaping products, and questions about her management experience.
Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, previously expressed serious concerns about Overton’s involvement in efforts to revise federal childhood vaccination recommendations.
Cassidy also questioned whether Overton possessed the leadership experience necessary to oversee the FDA, which regulates prescription medications, medical devices, food products, and tobacco products.
However, Cassidy disputed the administration’s decision to withdraw her nomination, arguing that negotiations with senators had created a possible path to confirmation.
The Louisiana Republican said his conversations with Overton had convinced him that she would prioritize scientific evidence and challenge decisions that could endanger public health.
Overton also faced scrutiny over her views on mifepristone, an FDA-approved abortion medication. She previously raised concerns about the drug but acknowledged during her confirmation hearing that it had satisfied the agency’s approval standards.
Anti-abortion organizations pressed the administration to secure stronger commitments regarding federal oversight of abortion medications before moving forward with her confirmation.
Meanwhile, activists opposing Overton’s nomination launched a public campaign criticizing her perceived support for flavored vaping products. Signs targeting the nominee appeared around Capitol Hill in the days leading up to the scheduled vote.
The controversy also exposed disagreements among advocates of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again initiative, with some questioning whether Overton would sufficiently challenge corporate interests.
Administration officials maintained that the FDA needs leadership aligned with Kennedy’s broader health agenda, emphasizing a renewed focus on public health and regulatory priorities.
The agency has operated under acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Makary’s departure, leaving one of the federal government’s most influential regulatory positions without a permanently confirmed leader.
Republican Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, a physician who recently lost his reelection campaign, has reportedly emerged as a possible replacement candidate.
The administration now faces a limited window to confirm another nominee before Democrats assume control of the Senate in January.
With Overton’s nomination withdrawn, President Trump must decide whether to pursue another confirmation effort or continue relying on acting leadership while the FDA implements the administration’s health policy priorities.

WASHINGTON, D.C. (LifeSiteNews) – The Trump administration confirmed on Tuesday that it has withdrawn the nomination of administration health policy adviser Dr. Heidi Overton to succeed Marty Makary as Commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), a position that has lacked a permanent holder since May.
Earlier this year, the White House confirmed Makary’s resignation amid a storm of issues with his tenure, including his handling of abortion pills and vaccines as well as internal staff turmoil. The role has since been temporarily filled by Deputy Commissioner for Food Kyle Diamantas, who insisted that he was pro-life amid concerns about a past assignment representing Planned Parenthood in a property dispute.
In August, President Donald Trump announced as his permanent choice Overton, currently deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, who served on the president’s Office of American Innovation and Domestic Policy Council in Trump’s first term.
Overton was initially met with optimism from pro-lifers, but in September questioning declined to reaffirm her past comments recognizing the danger of abortion pills, raising concerns about an issue on which the Trump administration was already facing pro-life discontent for slow-walking the restoration of rules that had been waived by the Biden administration.
On Tuesday, an administration official told Axios that Overton’s nomination has been pulled because she “lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation.”
NBC News adds that crucial votes such as Sens. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), Susan Collins (R-ME), and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) were still undecided as of last week, with Collins saying she still needed “to get some answers on various things.” Reporting cites doubts about Overton’s commitment to the pro-life and so-called “Make America Healthy Again” causes, as did questions about her experience level.
But following her withdrawal, Cassidy suggested deeper issues between the administration and pro-lifers were ultimately to blame.
“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton,” Cassidy wrote on X. “The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate. My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk.”
“The last issue was that pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues,” he continued. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments. Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”
In May 2025, the Trump administration promised a “complete review” of abortion pill safety data that pro-lifers hope might lead to a restoration of pre-Biden restrictions, but more than a year came and went without results while the administration resisted pro-life lawsuits to force an immediate rule change.
Last month, the FDA said it now expected the review to be complete by May 2027, feeding longstanding suspicions that the results were being delayed until after the midterm elections. However, any resulting pro-life policy change could still take until the final months of Trump’s presidency.

sources.news_title: Another Would-Be Trump FDA Administrator Goes Down Amid MAHA-MAGA Quagmire
sources.text:
The Trump administration’s latest attempt to confirm a leader of the Food and Drug Administration imploded Tuesday night, as the White House withdrew nominee Heidi Overton.
The administration’s FDA woes stretch back to May, when the second Trump term’s first administrator, Marty Makary, resigned under pressure. The role has not been filled on a permanent basis since.
To some degree, FDA nominees keep failing because of the same dynamics that have foiled two of President Donald Trump’s surgeon general picks and his first nominee to head the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The alliance between MAGA and MAHA is an uneasy one (the MAHA ethos borrowing from both the political left and right) and its primary tether — suspicion of or opposition to vaccines — made most of these nominees radioactive to the few traditional Republicans who remain in Congress. And unfortunately for the MAHA movement, virtually all of that endangered breed of Republican (Sens. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), Susan Collins (R-ME), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)) sit on the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) committee, which must first confirm all of these nominees before they get to the floor.
Overton was no exception, standing beside President Donald Trump (and reportedly helping draft) an executive order recommending that children get fewer vaccines, and that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines get broken up into separate shots.
Then there’s the abortion trap, an added pitfall for the FDA nominees in particular. Fierce opposition to abortion is much more traditionally right-wing than it is MAHA, but candidates must satisfy both camps to succeed.
Anti-abortion advocates have become increasingly incensed that the Trump White House didn’t do more to restrict mifepristone in its first two years (and, in fact, approved a second generic form of the drug under Makary). While Overton’s paper trail indicated a personal antipathy to abortion, her squishiness on the issue during her confirmation hearing inflamed the already short-tempered activists. Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, a major anti-abortion group, earlier this month called for Overton’s confirmation to be delayed until she committed to reimposing the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone (stopping the drug being sent to patients in the mail) and to slanting the FDA’s current “safety study” so it aligns with the group’s (false) insistence that the drug comes with significant medical risks.
But outwardly vowing to fulfill those demands would make it more difficult for Overton to secure the support of Collins and Murkowski, both of whom support abortion rights.
“[P]ro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues,” Cassidy wrote on Twitter Tuesday (though he maintained that Overton had the support to get through). “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.”
Makary ran into this problem too, facing blowback from the anti-abortion movement when it was reported that he urged the slow-walking of the mifepristone study so that it would conclude after the midterms, theoretically helping the administration avoid any electoral punishment.
As the administration scrambles for a replacement nominee, multiple outlets have reported that Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS), who just lost his reelection bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton, is being considered. (The White House, however, denied this to Politico).
Marshall, a former OB/GYN, both opposes abortion and heads the Senate MAHA caucus. But even he may find the MAGA-MAHA tightrope difficult to walk if he ultimately is nominated, or installed in an acting capacity. He reportedly opposes bans on the herbicide glyphosate, which runs afoul of MAHA’s strict litmus test.
IOW, Overton’s window just closed.
It’s kind of a problem when all your nominees for any position are manifestly unqualified and therefore face scrutiny on their qualifications and beliefs that are likely to be put into actions, and the do-nothing Congress disappears to be replaced by a (hopefully) active Congress that isn’t going to accept unqualified nominees.
The shit show starts at the top, and the sooner that changes the better.

sources.news_title: White House pulls Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination a day before committee vote
sources.text:
The White House has withdrawn Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a day before the Senate health committee was set to vote on it. Overton, a physician who grew up in Gallup, New Mexico, had faced questions from senators of both parties.
The White House said Tuesday it pulled the nomination amid growing indications she did not have the votes to win Senate confirmation, the Associated Press reported. CBS News, relying on an administration official and others with knowledge of the decision, reported that the committee had been scheduled to vote on Wednesday.
The arithmetic was tight. According to the AP, she needed all 12 of the committee's Republicans, since Democrats hold 11 seats on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) panel. Without the committee's backing, the AP reported, she faced little chance of a full Senate vote. The Hill noted that GOP leaders could have tried to bring her nomination directly to the floor, but that would likely have met significant obstacles.
Committee chairman Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican and a physician, disputed the White House's account late Tuesday. He said the problem was not that Overton lacked the votes, and that the White House had "abandoned a viable confirmation path," CBS News reported.
In a statement, Cassidy said "pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration's commitment to life issues," but the administration withdrew Overton instead. "I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate," he said. Two sources told CBS News that whip efforts to line up Republican votes were still underway when the White House shared its decision.
Cassidy had been a source of doubt earlier. The AP reported that he called Overton's support for President Donald Trump's plan to split combined vaccines such as the measles, mumps and rubella shot "almost disqualifying," and that he pressed her at a September hearing about her independence from Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The Hill reported that Overton declined at that hearing to say whether she would stand up to the president or Kennedy. Drug Topics reported that she did tell the panel the measles vaccine is safe and effective.
Abortion policy was a second point of friction. According to The Hill, Overton is openly anti-abortion. Drug Topics reported that she testified the drug is safe and effective as currently labeled, while The Hill reported she would not say directly whether she personally believes mifepristone is safe. Drug Topics added that Republicans were troubled by her noncommittal answers on the FDA's continuing safety review of it. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, questioned her about the drug, according to Searchlight New Mexico.
Vaping also played a role. The AP reported that Sen. Susan Collins of Maine raised concerns about Overton's approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The AP noted that the FDA recently authorized its first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers. CBS News reported that some lawmakers and administration allies were skeptical partly because of her execution of Trump's pro-vape policies. The AP added that prominent voices in the Make America Healthy Again movement opposed her too.
In New Mexico, the withdrawal was welcomed by at least one of her fellow graduates. Overton graduated from the University of New Mexico School of Medicine in 2015, and Searchlight New Mexico reported that more than 50 alumni had signed a letter objecting to her nomination. The letter argued that the agency's leader should have a policy record that aligns with "established clinical consensus and sound regulatory science," in the letter's words.
Dr. Mike Winer, an addiction medicine and family physician from the school's class of 2018, said the decision came as a relief. In a message to The New Mexican, he said the country needs a commissioner whose decisions are "grounded in science," among other qualities.
CBS News reported that the agency has had no Senate-confirmed head since Dr. Marty Makary's forced exit in May. It is now led on an acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, according to the AP. A source told CBS News earlier Tuesday that officials had already begun speaking with other possible picks, some of whom could serve as acting chief and skip Senate confirmation.
Time is short. CBS News reported that confirming any permanent commissioner would have to happen in the narrow window before Democrats take over the Senate in January. Cassidy, who lost his Republican primary in May and has only weeks left in his term, said "with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats." The AP reported that no timetable for a new nominee was immediately known.

New Mexico native withdrawn from consideration to lead FDA
NEW MEXICO — The White House withdrew Heidi Overton, a Gallup native and University of New Mexico graduate, from consideration to lead the Food and Drug Administration.
The White House withdrew her nomination Tuesday, about three months after announcing it.
The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee needed to sign off on Overton for her to move on to the full Senate. The committee consists of 12 Republicans and 11 Democrats, with Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., as the chairman.
If the Senate approved her with a simple majority, Overton would’ve led the FDA. She needed 50 senators plus the vice president or 51 senators voting yes. However, there were concerns about the votes – according to AP and lawmakers like Cassidy.
“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate,” Cassidy said.
Overton was valedictorian of her Gallup High School class. At UNM, she earned a bachelor’s degree in health, medicine and human values in 2011 and graduated from the university’s medical school in 2015.
Overton earned a doctorate at Johns Hopkins University in 2022. Her nomination received praise from at least one prominent New Mexico leader.
“Dr. Overton’s nomination is an incredible accomplishment and a proud moment for New Mexico,” said House Republican Leader Gail Armstrong, R-Magdalena. “Her New Mexico roots and experience in medicine and public service have prepared her for this important role. On behalf of the House Republican Caucus, we congratulate Dr. Overton and wish her the very best through the confirmation process.”
Overton’s nomination came as the FDA reviews abortion medication policies, including an ongoing safety study of mifepristone. Former FDA commissioner Marty Makary resigned in May. Makary faced criticism from some Republicans, including U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley, over his agency’s handling of mifepristone.
The Atlantic described Overton as “one of the most powerful public health officials” in Trump’s second term as a domestic policy official who briefs him on health issues. She first rose to prominence as a White House fellow in 2019 and later joined the America First Policy Institute.
While she was with the AFPI, Overton described the 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision to overturn Roe v. Wade as a “huge victory for life” and pushed for limits on access to abortion medications, including mifepristone and misoprostol.
The Democratic Party of New Mexico sharply criticized Overton’s nomination in a statement.
“Sadly, it appears that Trump selected an individual who will only continue his FDA’s agenda of restricting reproductive rights, promoting anti-vaccine policies, and increasing foodborne disease outbreaks. But we expect nothing less from Donald Trump, who has consistently made the least serious and most unqualified political appointments of any president in American history, than to appoint an unqualified, anti-abortion activist like Heidi Overton to such a critical position,” the party stated.
There is no word on who the White House will put forth instead as a pick for FDA commissioner.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn’t have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation.
Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for President Donald Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA, following a tumultuous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary.
But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his administration’s approach to vaccines.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday morning.
Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot — “almost disqualifying.” And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to disagree with Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic.
But late Tuesday night, Cassidy suggested he had been prepared to back Overton and suggested her nomination was derailed by disagreements over abortion, not vaccines.
“I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate,” Cassidy stated in a posting on X.
He went on to say that anti-abortion Republicans had sought commitments on “life issues” from the White House, but “the Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.”
Currently, the FDA is conducting a safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone — at the request of Trump — that could reinstate restrictions on the drug’s use, including a requirement for in-person prescribing. FDA has promised a report on its safety findings by March.
To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on the chamber floor.
Republicans have been racing to try to confirm Trump’s nominees before handing over power to Senate Democrats in January.
It was not immediately clear when, or if, the White House might put forward another nominee.
Cassidy has previously threatened to oppose health nominees
Cassidy has repeatedly tried to win commitments on upholding vaccine standards, including from Kennedy, by threatening to withhold his vote. Ultimately, though, he voted in favor of each nominee that came before his committee.
Other Republicans, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, raised concerns about other health issues, including Overton’s approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The FDA recently authorized the first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers looking to quit. Under previous administrations, including the first Trump administration, the agency had opposed vaping flavors that could attract teens and children.
Opposition to Overton’s nomination also came from influential figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, who blamed her and other White House officials for sidelining some of Kennedy’s top health goals, including crackdowns on food additives and pesticides.
Earlier this month, Calley Means told Joe Rogan that White House aides, including Overton, worked within the administration to advance a Supreme Court decision blocking thousands of lawsuits over the weedkiller glyphosate. Means, a former Kennedy aide who recently left the government, said that and other key decisions were carried out at the behest of industry lobbyists.
“There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for,” Means said.
Trump has pulled back several other health nominations
Trump’s first nominee for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. David Weldon, was replaced because it was unclear he had enough Republican support to be confirmed. Two of Trump’s surgeon general nominees, including Dr. Casey Means — Calley Means’ sister — were also pulled after facing pushback from Senate Republicans and most Democrats.
The FDA is currently being led on an acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, an attorney and friend of Donald Trump Jr. He was elevated to the post in May after previously serving as the agency’s top food official. Under federal rules, acting officials are limited to about seven months leading a federal agency.
The FDA under Makary was marked by a string of scientific disputes, leadership changes and media stories detailing low morale and internal dysfunction among staffers. The FDA has lost about 20% of its employees to layoffs, buyouts, retirements or resignations since Trump took office.

The senior administration official told the outlet that the White House wanted to “go in a new direction at FDA” while continuing to support Kennedy’s health agenda.
“The decision means the Trump administration will have to find a new candidate to lead the FDA,” Axios said.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The White House is dropping Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official confirmed Tuesday.
The decision comes a day before the Senate Health Committee was scheduled to vote on whether to advance her nomination to the full Senate for confirmation.
Axios first reported the White House’s decision.
The move follows weeks of doubts from key Republicans on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. To advance to the full Senate, Overton would have needed 11 votes in the 21-member committee, meaning she couldn’t afford to lose a single Republican if all Democrats opposed her.
Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the committee’s chairman, had questioned whether Overton — a preventive medicine doctor who serves as a domestic policy official in the White House — had enough experience to lead the agency.
Prior to joining the White House, Overton worked as chief policy officer at the conservative think tank America First Policy Institute.
Before Overton’s confirmation hearing in September, Cassidy wrote on X that he had “strong concerns” about her nomination, saying her lack of managerial experience left her poorly prepared to lead the agency. In a post last week, Cassidy said he remained undecided.
On Tuesday night, Cassidy criticized the White House for pulling Overton’s nomination.
“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton,” Cassidy, a physician, wrote on X. “My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk.”
“The last issue was that pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues. The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” said Cassidy, who is leaving Congress in early January. “Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, told NBC News last week that she was undecided and had “not taken a position,” saying she needed “to get some answers on various things.”
Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska declined last week to say how she’d vote. During the confirmation hearing, Murkowski asked Overton about political pressure surrounding access to mifepristone, and criticized Overton for not taking a clear position on the subject.
Overton has praised the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade and called for strict restrictions on medication abortion.
The FDA is set to finish its safety review of mifepristone in March, one of the most consequential decisions the agency faces.
Overton’s nomination was already working against a tight window. Democrats take control of the Senate in early January, when she would have had to be renominated if she weren’t confirmed in this Congress. Her chances of being confirmed under a Democratic-controlled Senate would be slim.
The FDA has been without a permanent commissioner since Dr. Marty Makary resigned in May, in part because of the administration’s decision to authorize several fruit-flavored vaping products.
The vacancy adds to a long period of upheaval at the nation’s top health agencies.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention went nearly a year without a permanent director after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed Susan Monarez just 29 days into the job last year. Trump’s first pick for that role, former congressman Dave Weldon, couldn’t secure enough Republican support, and the agency cycled through a series of acting leaders before the Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz in August.

sources.text:
The White House is dropping President Donald Trump’s nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) amid a lack of congressional support, as Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) is reportedly being considered as a potential replacement.
Axios reported Tuesday evening that the White House had decided to drop Overton’s nomination ahead of a scheduled Wednesday vote by the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
According to a Tuesday report from Semafor, four people familiar with the matter said Republicans are discussing Marshall as a possible replacement for Overton, whose nomination has encountered resistance from both anti-abortion activists and moderate Republicans.
Marshall, a physician who lost his reelection bid earlier this month, is reportedly viewed as a stronger candidate for Senate confirmation as Republicans face a narrowing window to approve Trump’s nominees before Democrats assume control of the Senate in January.
“Marshall is viewed as an alternative if Heidi can’t make it through,” a Trump administration official told Semafor. “Senators have an easier time getting confirmed, traditionally. At this point, it’s hard to get anyone approved.”
“There is a growing view in the Senate that a senator would be the only person while we’ve got a majority, so Roger Marshall’s name is quickly percolating as a person who would be confirmable,” a senior Republican aide told Semafor.
It remains unclear whether the White House will pursue Marshall or another potential nominee if Overton’s confirmation efforts fail, particularly given the limited time remaining before Republicans lose their Senate majority.
The White House did not immediately comment on the matter, according to Semafor, while Marshall’s office declined to comment.
The FDA has operated without a permanent commissioner since former Commissioner Marty Makary was pushed out in May after disagreements with the White House over whether to authorize flavored vaping products. Makary also faced pressure from anti-abortion Republicans seeking additional restrictions on mifepristone, a drug used in medication abortions.
Following Makary’s departure, Kyle Diamantas, an attorney who previously served as the FDA’s top food official, was selected as acting commissioner. According to Semafor, Diamantas earned a reputation as a competent administrator who helped stabilize the agency.
However, a Trump administration official told Semafor that Diamantas, who did not want the commissioner’s position permanently, is weighing a departure from the FDA regardless of the outcome of Overton’s nomination.
As Breitbart News reported on November 3, Marshall lost his reelection bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor, in a race widely considered a tossup. NBC News called the race for Hamilton, making him the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas since 1932. Hamilton has previously stated that he believes the Bible contains errors, that Christians are not required to believe in Jesus’s virgin birth, that pagans who never believed in Jesus will nevertheless be saved by him, and that he can determine where the Apostle Paul was wrong in scripture. By Adam Cancryn, Sarah Owermohle, CNN
(CNN) — The White House abruptly pulled its nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration late Tuesday amid what Trump officials saw as skepticism from multiple Senate Republicans, a White House official and two other people familiar with the matter told CNN.
The decision to drop the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton, a senior White House aide, came the night before a Senate committee was due to vote on whether to advance her nomination.
The committee’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy, maintained Tuesday night that she was on the verge of garnering enough support.
“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton,” Cassidy wrote in a post on X shortly after her nomination was pulled. “This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate.”
The White House did not immediately comment on Cassidy’s contention. But officials’ decision to pull Overton’s nomination marked the culmination of weeks of intensifying scrutiny over her ability from both Republican senators and activists aligned with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Trump officials had spent recent days working to fend off threats to sink Overton’s nomination by conservative Sen. Josh Hawley and the broader anti-abortion movement, which has been infuriated by the administration’s lack of urgency in restricting distribution of mifepristone, two people familiar with the matter said.
At the same time, Overton faced concerns from abortion rights proponents Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski over her strident support for anti-abortion policies and role in the administration’s approval of flavored vapes.
Her nomination also exposed fault lines between the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, led by Kennedy, and more traditional conservative circles.
As a senior White House domestic policy aide, Overton spent the past year and a half as the main conduit between HHS leaders working to advance a handful of key MAHA policies and top Trump White House officials who have stalled them in recent months — sowing frustration and distrust within the broader MAHA movement.
Though Kennedy praised her nomination in August, those familiar with the dynamics between them have described the relationship as less than close.
Asked shortly after her selection for FDA commissioner about Overton’s relationship with Kennedy, one person familiar with the dynamic bluntly characterized it as “not good.”
Another called their interactions “icy.”
“She’s not MAHA,” said the second person familiar with the dynamic.
Nevertheless, Cassidy contended on Tuesday that Overton had a path to confirmation, writing that “pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues.”
“The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” he added.
Overton is just the latest health care nominee to be pulled amid crumbling GOP support; the White House has also yanked nominees to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the surgeon general’s office as moderate Republicans voiced concerns.
The move is now likely to leave the FDA without a permanent leader well into next year. In his X post, Cassidy appeared to rule out considering another nominee before Republicans lose control of the Senate in January, writing: “Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”
A nomination in trouble
When Overton met privately with Cassidy, the outgoing Louisiana senator and physician, last week, the discussion had seemed to go well for the nominee.
She and her team emerged from the high-stakes sit-down confident in her candidacy for the top health job, two people briefed on the matter said, and Cassidy scheduled the committee vote for her shortly afterward, though he did not publicly endorse her.
But signs of fracturing support for her soon emerged. In the past week, posters have been popping up across Washington, DC, neighborhoods, urging senators to “say no to Heidi Vaperton for FDA commissioner,” claiming she is “pro-big tobacco” and “pro-abortion ban.”
The posters were organized by Health in Office, a nonpartisan group concerned about the administration’s health agenda, as The Washington Post first reported. The group’s spokesperson Jenny Kay declined to say who funded the project but said the activists behind the project have “a lot of concerns around who has already been put in charge of the health of people in this country.”
Despite their meeting last week, Cassidy signaled as recently as Sunday that a question mark hung over her nomination.

“I still have questions, and so I cannot tell you the outcome of that vote right now.”
Collins, another key Republican whose vote was needed, had also been publicly noncommittal about her vote. During Overton’s confirmation hearing, she questioned the nominee about her stance on flavored vapes, following reports that there were disagreements between the White House and former FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary over greenlighting fruity e-cigarettes. The dispute ultimately led to the commissioner’s exit in May.
The disputes over vapes were recently resurfaced in a lengthy podcast interview with Calley Means, a MAHA advocate and White House senior adviser who left the administration in October.
Overton, a doctor by training who then worked in public policy, worked to “relax standards on fruit flavored vapes,” he told “The Joe Rogan Experience.”
He also accused Overton, who was closely aligned with former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, of putting corporate interests ahead of the MAHA health agenda.
Wiles’ support was critical in Overton’s selection to lead the FDA earlier this year, people familiar with the matter said. But since Wiles’ departure and replacement with Stephen Miller, the new chief of staff has moved quickly to put his stamp on the administration, including signaling greater support for Kennedy and the MAHA coalition that has long been skeptical of Overton’s candidacy.
There had also been internal rifts between Kennedy and Overton over glyphosate and other stalled MAHA goals, according to two people familiar with policy discussions.
Overton has not publicly commented on Means’ allegations. HHS did not respond to a request for comment.

But it’s unclear whether Trump would pick him — and if he could win over enough of his Senate colleagues to be confirmed.
Marshall is a member of the Senate’s health committee and benefits from close relationships on the panel. But he has been one of the most ardent supporters of the Trump administration’s divisive “Make America Healthy Again” policies, including questioning the safety of vaccines in hearings that have pitted him against the committee’s chair, Cassidy, and other moderate Republicans.
In the hours after the news of Overton’s withdrawal, some MAHA advocates celebrated.
Vani Hari, a healthy food advocate known by her “Food Babe” blog, wrote on X: “Another one bites the dust.”

The prospect of Overton taking the top post at the FDA had alarmed abortion-rights supporters because she has celebrated abortion bans and refused to say whether she believes birth control is a form of abortion.
Standing in front of Americans for Contraception’s “FREEDA Womb,” a 20-foot-tall inflatable IUD, at Portland City Hall on Tuesday, Mark Gallagher, a 54-year-old Kennebunk resident, said the government has no right to restrict access to contraception for his two teenage daughters.
“I want them to make a decision about their own bodies,” said Gallagher, who identified himself as a Catholic. “I want them to be assisted and guided by doctors and scientists, and not Republicans in Congress, and certainly not the Trump administration.”
Collins’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment late Tuesday night about Overton’s withdrawal. Last week, she told NBC News she had not yet taken a position.
Overton has been a vocal opponent of medication abortion and celebrated the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision that overturned Roe v. Wade. She serves as a White House policy adviser at a time when the administration is questioning the safety of certain drugs and vaccines.
Maine Rep. Anne Graham, D-North Yarmouth, a retired pediatric nurse practitioner, had called on Collins to oppose the nomination.
“Sen. Collins needs to stand up for the women of Maine, particularly rural women, who would not be able to access birth control under Overton’s oversight,” Graham said at the news conference Tuesday.

Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for President Donald Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA, following a tumultuous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary.
But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his administration’s approach to vaccines.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday morning.
Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot — “almost disqualifying.” And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to disagree with Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic.
But late Tuesday night, Cassidy suggested he had been prepared to back Overton and suggested her nomination was derailed by disagreements over abortion, not vaccines.
“I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate,” Cassidy stated in a posting on X.
He went on to say that anti-abortion Republicans had sought commitments on “life issues” from the White House, but “the Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.”
Currently, the FDA is conducting a safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone — at the request of Trump — that could reinstate restrictions on the drug’s use, including a requirement for in-person prescribing. FDA has promised a report on its safety findings by March.
To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on the chamber floor.
Republicans have been racing to try to confirm Trump’s nominees before handing over power to Senate Democrats in January.
It was not immediately clear when, or if, the White House might put forward another nominee.
Cassidy has previously threatened to oppose health nominees
Cassidy has repeatedly tried to win commitments on upholding vaccine standards, including from Kennedy, by threatening to withhold his vote. Ultimately, though, he voted in favor of each nominee that came before his committee.
Other Republicans, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, raised concerns about other health issues, including Overton’s approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The FDA recently authorized the first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers looking to quit. Under previous administrations, including the first Trump administration, the agency had opposed vaping flavors that could attract teens and children.
Opposition to Overton’s nomination also came from influential figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, who blamed her and other White House officials for sidelining some of Kennedy’s top health goals, including crackdowns on food additives and pesticides.
Earlier this month, Calley Means told Joe Rogan that White House aides, including Overton, worked within the administration to advance a Supreme Court decision blocking thousands of lawsuits over the weedkiller glyphosate. Means, a former Kennedy aide who recently left the government, said that and other key decisions were carried out at the behest of industry lobbyists.
“There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for,” Means said.
Trump has pulled back several other health nominations
Trump’s first nominee for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. David Weldon, was replaced because it was unclear he had enough Republican support to be confirmed. Two of Trump’s surgeon general nominees, including Dr. Casey Means — Calley Means’ sister — were also pulled after facing pushback from Senate Republicans and most Democrats.
The FDA is currently being led on an acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, an attorney and friend of Donald Trump Jr. He was elevated to the post in May after previously serving as the agency’s top food official. Under federal rules, acting officials are limited to about seven months leading a federal agency.
The FDA under Makary was marked by a string of scientific disputes, leadership changes and media stories detailing low morale and internal dysfunction among staffers. The FDA has lost about 20% of its employees to layoffs, buyouts, retirements or resignations since Trump took office.

Trump’s pick Heidi Overton dropped as nominee for FDA commissioner
The White House has dropped Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, an official confirmed to ABC News.
Overton's nomination faced an uphill battle with GOP senators, per sources familiar with committee Republicans' thinking. Multiple Republican senators were concerned with Overton's stances on abortion, vaccines and vaping.
Overton was nominated in August by President Donald Trump, who described her in a post on social media as a "ROCKSTAR in my Administration."
Viewed as a Trump loyalist, Overton is White House deputy director of Domestic Policy. It's unclear when the president will nominate a new choice for FDA commissioner and if the Senate will work to confirm the new nominee during a lame duck session.
The agency has been without a permanent leader for nearly seven months. Marty Makary resigned in April over clashes with the White House over the authorization of fruit-flavored vapes.
Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas is temporarily leading the agency.
Axios was the first to report that Overton's nomination was being dropped.
She was due for a vote in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) committee this week.
In a statement on social media Tuesday evening, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., who chairs the committee, said he believes Overton's nomination would've had the votes to not only pass through committee but a full Senate vote.
"The [White House] said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass," Cassidy said. "This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate."
Cassidy said the sticking point was a request from anti-abortion Republican senators for final assurances from the administration on its commitment to abortion-related policies.
"The last issue was that pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration's commitment to life issues. The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.
He contended that given the limited time left in this Congressional session, confirmation of a new FDA Commissioner will now be at the hands of Senate Democrats.
At her September nomination hearing, Cassidy expressed concerns with Overton participating in Trump's executive order overhauling the childhood vaccine schedule and suggested that she couldn't be disloyal to Trump.
However, in his statement on Tuesday Cassidy said his conversations with Overton "convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk."
At the confirmation hearing, Overton also faced bipartisan criticism about her vaping and anti-abortion stances from Republican Sens. Susan Collins, of Maine, and Ashley Moody, of Florida, and Democratic Sen. Patty Murray, of Washington.
At the September hearing, Moody pressed Overton about illicit vapes allegedly being smuggled from China and given to kids.
"Within your power at the FDA will you commit to examining regulations currently in place and making sure that we are modifying them as necessary to prohibit, crack down on illicit Chinese vapes?" Moody asked.
Overton vowed to crack down on products that are "affecting kids." She also stressed that there is "100% agreement" from the Trump administration on protecting kids from illegal substances, vapes and flavored vapes.
Murray has labeled Overton an "anti-abortion extremist." She criticized Overton for waffling on questions about the mifepristone abortion pill and dodging whether using birth control is considered a form of abortion.
Mini Timmaraju, Reproductive Freedom for All President and CEO, celebrated the White House's decision to pull the nomination.
"Heidi Overton posed a serious threat to the future of medication abortion access," Timmaraju said in a statement.
